foundational.authors: Brand, James, Ayelet Israeli, and Donald Ngwe
foundational.title: Using LLMs for Market Research
foundational.tldr: Asks whether LLMs can help researchers understand consumer preferences, focusing on the distribution of responses by querying GPT-3.5 for hundreds of survey answers per prompt. The responses agree with economic theory and documented consumer behavior, including downward sloping demand curves and state dependence. Willingness to pay estimates for products and features are realistic in size and comparable to those from a recent survey of human consumers. Offers preliminary guidelines for querying GPT-3.5 in marketing and discusses limitations.

foundational.title: Frontiers: Can Large Language Models Capture Human Preferences?
foundational.label: utd24
foundational.tldr: Asks whether GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can stand in for human survey respondents when eliciting intertemporal preferences, comparing their choices between smaller sooner and larger later rewards with human responses in several languages. Both models are less patient than humans: GPT-3.5 shows a lexicographic preference for earlier rewards, and GPT-4 has substantially higher discount rates. The models appear more patient in languages with weak future tense marking, such as German and Mandarin. Asking the model to explain its choices narrows, but does not close, the gap with humans.

foundational.authors: Arora, Neeraj, Ishita Chakraborty, and Yohei Nishimura
foundational.title: AI–Human Hybrids for Marketing Research: Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) as Collaborators
foundational.label: utd24
foundational.tldr: Examines how combining humans and LLMs can make marketing research faster and more effective, using GPT-4 to replicate a 2019 study with qualitative and quantitative parts for a Fortune 500 food company. In qualitative work, LLMs generate sample profiles, synthetic respondents and interviews, yielding richer data than humans alone and matching humans at identifying themes and summarizing. Expert judges find the hybrid beats either alone. In quantitative work, the LLM gets the direction and sentiment of answers right, and quality improves with few shot prompting and retrieval augmented generation.

foundational.authors: Ye, Zikun, Hema Yoganarasimhan, and Yufeng Zheng
foundational.title: LOLA: LLM-Assisted Online Learning Algorithm for Content Experiments
foundational.label: utd24
foundational.tldr: Asks how to identify the most engaging headlines, using 17,681 headline A/B tests from Upworthy. Purely LLM approaches fall short: prompting performs poorly, and OpenAI embeddings and a fine tuned Llama-3-8B are only slightly better than random. Proposes LOLA, which pairs the best LLM approach with an Upper Confidence Bound algorithm that adjusts traffic over time to maximize clicks. LOLA beats standard A/B testing, pure bandit algorithms and LLM methods alone, especially when experimental traffic is limited.

foundational.title: Database Report: Twin-2K-500: A Data Set for Building Digital Twins of over 2,000 People Based on Their Answers to over 500 Questions
foundational.label: utd24
foundational.tldr: Releases a public dataset for building and testing LLM digital twins, addressing the lack of large public data on individual behavior. A representative sample of 2,058 Americans spent 2.42 hours on average answering more than 500 questions over four waves, covering demographics, psychology, economics, personality and cognition, plus replications of behavioral economics experiments and a pricing survey. The final wave repeats earlier tasks to give a retest baseline. Initial analyses suggest high data quality and support for twins that predict behavior well for individuals and groups.

categories.name: Consumer Simulation

entries.title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
entries.tldr: Asks whether a language model can stand in for specific human subpopulations in social science research. Conditions GPT-3 on sociodemographic backstories of real participants in large US surveys to create 'silicon samples' and compares their answers with the human responses. The match goes beyond surface similarity and reflects how ideas, attitudes and sociocultural context relate within each group. Argues that the model's bias is fine grained and tied to demographics, so proper conditioning can reproduce response patterns across many groups.

entries.title: Can AI language models replace human participants?
entries.tldr: Asks whether and when language models such as GPT could replace human participants in psychological science. Starts from recent work showing that these models make humanlike judgments across a number of domains. Reviews this early research, presents a theoretical model of the question, and outlines the caveats of using AI as a participant in place of people.

entries.authors: Aher, Gati V., Rosa I. Arriaga, and Adam Tauman Kalai
entries.title: Using Large Language Models to Simulate Multiple Humans and Replicate Human Subject Studies
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Proposes the Turing Experiment, which tests how well a language model such as GPT can simulate a representative sample of people rather than one individual, as in the Turing Test. Uses it to replicate four classic studies from economics, psycholinguistics, and social psychology: the Ultimatum Game, Garden Path Sentences, the Milgram Shock Experiment, and Wisdom of Crowds. The first three replications reproduce the original findings. The last reveals a "hyper-accuracy distortion" in some models, including ChatGPT and GPT-4, that could affect applications in education and the arts.

entries.title: Frontiers: Determining the Validity of Large Language Models for Automated Perceptual Analysis
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Asks whether large language models can substitute for human participants in market research, focusing on perceptual analysis. Proposes a method that produces perceptual analyses from LLM responses using both brand similarity measures and product attribute ratings. Agreement between the human and LLM datasets exceeds 75%. For some product categories, full or partial automation could make market research faster and possibly cheaper, and as models train on larger corpora they may answer more nuanced questions tied to demographics or context.

entries.title: The Case for Synthetic Data
entries.tldr: Weighs which uses of synthetic data in marketing research the current evidence supports. Argues that LLM respondents prompted with basic demographics give generic answers, while digital twins reach reasonable accuracy in some domains, such as predicting purchases of existing products, and capture segment patterns better than individuals. Rejects using synthetic respondents to fill quota shortfalls, since this masks uncertainty and creates false precision. Concludes that LLMs can widen the exploration of segments and concepts but should not soon replace human respondents.

entries.title: Large language models can predict the results of social science experiments
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLMs can predict the results of social science experiments, including studies absent from their training data. Uses an archive of 70 preregistered, nationally representative US survey experiments (469 effects, 119,330 participants), with GPT-4 simulating American samples responding to each study's stimuli. Predicted treatment effects correlate strongly with actual ones, match the accuracy of pooled human forecasts and hold for unpublished studies, though effect sizes are systematically overestimated. A survey of 460 social scientists maps likely uses and risks.

entries.title: Large language models outperform humans at estimating society’s everyday norms
entries.tldr: Asks how well large language models estimate American social norms in everyday situations. Compares six LLMs with 320 humans on 555 everyday scenarios. The models are highly accurate and beat the average individual, but their errors are systematic and shared across models, so averaging them adds little. Human errors are idiosyncratic and cancel out when averaged, and combining human and LLM estimates beats either source alone.

entries.authors: Horton, John J., Apostolos Filippas, and Benjamin S. Manning
entries.title: Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
entries.tldr: Asks whether large language models, because of how they are trained, can serve as implicit computational models of humans, called Homo silicus, for economic research. Gives LLMs endowments, information and preferences, then simulates their behavior in scenarios adapted from earlier experiments. The simulations produce results qualitatively similar to the original human studies, and where they diverge, the differences point to directions for further research. Discusses applications and conceptual issues of using such simulations to learn about real people.

entries.title: LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLM agents built from people's own interview and survey answers can predict their attitudes and behavior without training data for each outcome. Builds agents for 1,052 Americans from interviews, structured surveys, or both. On General Social Survey items withheld from the agents, they reach 82 to 86% of participants' own consistency when retested two weeks later, versus 74% for agents given only demographics. The agents also predict personality, economic game behavior and experimental responses, and narrow accuracy gaps across racial and ideological groups.

entries.authors: Lira, Benjamin, Noah Castelo, Stefano Puntoni, and Olivier Toubia
entries.title: Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity
entries.tldr: Tests whether brief conversations with AI chatbots that represent the political outgroup can substitute for contact across party lines. In five preregistered studies with 3,960 US partisans, people avoid an AI outgroup partner less than a human one, and a single ten-minute chat corrects misperceptions of the other side and warms feelings toward it. Participants who discuss immigration with an outgroup bot are six percentage points more likely to choose a real conversation with a partisan opponent, though the warmth effect mostly fades within a week.

entries.authors: France, Stephen L., and Pia A. Albinsson
entries.title: Synthetic Consumer Insight Generation with Large Language Models
entries.tldr: Tests whether large language models can produce synthetic consumer data for projective techniques, which aim to uncover consumers' associations, emotions, wants, and needs. Compares LLM responses across several projective tasks, models, prompting strategies, and temperature settings with human responses from a study of city tourism destinations, using linguistic measures, diversity metrics, and topic models. Broad topics and associations overlap substantially, but style, linguistic structure, and the way diversity arises differ notably. Closes with recommendations on model and prompt choices and on the limits of the approach.

entries.title: Customer Digital Twins in the Field: Cross-Sell Micro-Personalization at Scale

entries.authors: Nitsch, Felix J., Luca M. Lüpken, Nils Lüschow, and Tobias Kalenscher
entries.title: On the reliability of individual economic rationality measurements
entries.tldr: Asks whether measures of individual economic rationality, widely used to find psychological and neural correlates, are reliable in a psychometric sense. Draws on several published datasets with more than 1,600 participants. The measures show moderate to poor reliability by common standards, mainly because people differ little from one another rather than because measurement error is high. Since much of the field relies on correlational designs, this makes it hard to find sociodemographic or neural predictors of rationality.

entries.title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Asks whose opinions language models reflect when they answer subjective questions. Uses public opinion polls to build OpinionQA, a dataset that compares LM opinions with those of 60 US demographic groups on topics from abortion to automation. Current LMs show substantial misalignment with these groups, comparable to the gap between Democrats and Republicans on climate change, and it persists even when models are steered toward a group. Models tuned with human feedback lean left, and groups such as people aged 65 and older and widowed individuals are poorly reflected.

entries.title: Frontiers: Can Large Language Models Capture Human Preferences?
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Asks whether GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can stand in for human survey respondents when eliciting intertemporal preferences, comparing their choices between smaller sooner and larger later rewards with human responses in several languages. Both models are less patient than humans: GPT-3.5 shows a lexicographic preference for earlier rewards, and GPT-4 has substantially higher discount rates. The models appear more patient in languages with weak future tense marking, such as German and Mandarin. Asking the model to explain its choices narrows, but does not close, the gap with humans.

entries.title: Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models
entries.tldr: Tests how accurately ChatGPT can recover public opinion when prompted to adopt different personas and rate 11 sociopolitical groups on feeling thermometers. Average synthetic scores closely match the 2016–2020 American National Election Study (ANES). However, responses vary less than in real surveys, and regression coefficients often differ significantly from ANES estimates. Results also shift with small changes in prompt wording and differ for the same prompt over three months, raising concerns about the quality, reliability and reproducibility of synthetic survey data.

entries.title: The Illusion of Artificial Inclusion
entries.tldr: Surveys proposals to replace human participants in AI development, psychological science and user research with generative AI surrogates. A scoping review finds the recent wave of such proposals is motivated by cutting research and development costs and increasing the diversity of collected data. Argues that these proposals ignore and conflict with core values of work with human participants: representation, inclusion and understanding. Examines the principles behind human participation to chart future work that centers and empowers participants.

entries.title: Perils and opportunities in using large language models in psychological research
entries.tldr: Examines the limitations, ethical implications and potential of LLMs in psychological research, where they serve as models of the human psyche or as general text analysis tools. Warns against uncritical use, termed "GPTology", and shows its concrete impact across several empirical studies. The results point to the need to recognize global psychological diversity and caution against treating LLMs, especially in zero-shot settings, as universal solutions for text analysis. Calls for transparent, open methods and more diverse human samples instead of overreliance on LLMs.

entries.title: Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models
entries.tldr: Measures cultural bias in five OpenAI models, GPT-3 through GPT-4o, by comparing their answers with nationally representative survey data. All models express cultural values resembling those of English-speaking and Protestant European countries. Tests cultural prompting as a way to raise cultural alignment for each country and territory. For GPT-4, GPT-4-turbo, and GPT-4o, cultural prompting improves alignment for 71 to 81% of countries and territories, and ongoing evaluation is recommended alongside it.

entries.title: Towards Measuring the Representation of Subjective Global Opinions in Language Models
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Asks whose views LLM answers to subjective questions on global issues most resemble. Introduces GlobalOpinionQA, built from survey questions and answers collected across countries, and a metric that compares model responses with human responses by country, applied to a model trained with Constitutional AI. By default, responses are closer to populations such as the USA and some European and South American countries. Asking the model to take a given country's perspective shifts answers toward that population but can reflect harmful cultural stereotypes, and translating questions does not necessarily help.

entries.authors: Dominguez-Olmedo, Ricardo, Moritz Hardt, and Celestine Mendler-Dünner
entries.title: Questioning the Survey Responses of Large Language Models
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Examines how language models answer the American Community Survey from the US Census Bureau. Across 43 models and standard prompting methods, responses are driven by ordering and labeling biases, such as favoring answers labeled 'A'. Once answer order is randomized to correct for these biases, models trend toward uniformly random responses regardless of size or training data. This can make models seem to best represent the subgroups whose aggregate statistics happen to be closest to uniform, which can mislead conclusions about alignment.

entries.title: Large language models display human-like social desirability biases in Big Five personality surveys
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLMs show social desirability bias when they answer Big Five personality surveys. Varying how many questions a model sees reveals that models infer when they are being evaluated and then shift toward desirable traits, such as higher extraversion and lower neuroticism. The bias appears in every model tested, including GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 3, Llama 3 and PaLM-2, and is large: GPT-4 responses shift by 1.20 human standard deviations. It survives question reordering and paraphrasing, which limits the use of LLMs as proxies for human participants.

entries.authors: Wang, Angelina, Jamie Morgenstern, and John P. Dickerson
entries.title: Large language models that replace human participants can harmfully misportray and flatten identity groups
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Argues that LLMs used in place of human participants tend to misportray demographic groups and flatten the differences within them, because of two limitations in how current models are trained. Tests this on four LLMs with human studies of 3,200 participants across 16 demographic identities, and adds that identity prompts can essentialize identities. Links each limitation to a history of epistemic injustice that harms marginalized groups. Where replacement may still be worthwhile, techniques applied at inference time reduce but do not remove these harms.

entries.title: Machine Bias. How Do Generative Language Models Answer Opinion Polls?
entries.tldr: Examines how closely generative language models can emulate respondents in opinion polls, a use on which there is no scientific consensus. Finds that, to date, models cannot replace human subjects in opinion or attitude research. Their answers show strong bias and low variance on each topic, and that bias varies randomly from one topic to the next. Defines this pattern as machine bias and explores its consequences for research based on LLMs.

entries.title: Prompt architecture induces methodological artifacts in large language models
entries.tldr: Examines how 'prompt architecture', the seemingly arbitrary way a prompt is posed, shapes LLM responses. Five large full factorial experiments with GPT-3, GPT-4 and Llama 3.1 on standard similarity evaluation tasks show that order, labels, framing and justification interact to produce response order and label biases. Telling the model that items were randomized does not help, and uncommon labels reduce label bias but worsen order bias in GPT-4. Aggregating prompts generated from a full factorial design removes both biases.

entries.title: Large Language Models Assume People are More Rational than We Really are
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Asks whether the implicit models of human decision making in LLMs capture how people actually choose. Comparing model simulations and predictions with a large dataset of human decisions shows that GPT-4o, GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-3 8B and 70B, and Claude 3 Opus assume people are more rational than they are, aligning more closely with expected value theory than with real behavior. On another dataset, the inferences LLMs and people draw from others' decisions are highly correlated, so the models mirror the human expectation of rationality rather than actual behavior.

entries.title: Take caution in using LLMs as human surrogates
entries.tldr: Asks whether LLMs can serve as surrogates for human participants in social science research. Measures reasoning depth with the 11-20 money request game across many models. Nearly all advanced approaches fail to reproduce the distribution of human behavior, and the causes of failure vary and are hard to predict, involving input language, assigned roles, and safety safeguards. The results argue for caution, since LLMs rely on statistical patterns in text and lack the embodied experience that shapes human thinking.

entries.authors: Cui, Ziyan, Ning Li, and Huaikang Zhou
entries.title: A large-scale replication of scenario-based experiments in psychology and management using large language models
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Tests how well LLMs replicate scenario experiments from leading social science journals. Reruns 156 experiments with three leading LLMs. Main effects replicate at rates of 73–81% and interaction effects at 46–63%, but effect sizes are consistently larger than in human studies, and studies on race, gender and ethics replicate far less often. Where original studies found null results, LLMs produce significant findings 68–83% of the time, so they suit pilot testing and quick hypothesis checks but should supplement, not replace, human participants.

entries.title: Six Fallacies in Substituting Large Language Models for Human Participants
entries.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
entries.tldr: Evaluates the view that LLMs can replace human participants in behavioral and psychological research. Identifies six fallacies, such as equating token prediction with human intelligence, treating LLMs as an average human, and substituting model data for human evidence. Separates similarity in outputs from similarity in processes and offers safeguards for each fallacy. Concludes that LLMs are best treated as simulation tools for role play, rapid hypothesis testing and computational modeling, validated against human data, not as replacements for participants.

entries.title: Simulating human well-being with large language models: Systematic validation and misestimation across 64,000 individuals from 64 countries
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLMs can predict subjective well-being across global populations. Benchmarks four leading LLMs against self-reports and regression models, using natural language profiles of 64,000 individuals in 64 countries. The models reproduce known correlates such as income and health but underperform regressions, with the largest errors in underrepresented countries. A preregistered experiment shows that they rely on surface linguistic associations; adding context reduces these biases without removing them, so LLM estimates should not replace self-reported well-being.

entries.authors: Li, Ang, Haozhe Chen, Hongseok Namkoong, and Tianyi Peng
entries.title: LLM Generated Persona is a Promise with a Catch
entries.venue: NeurIPS 2025, Position Paper Track, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Takes the position that LLM persona generation, used to simulate human behavior in social science, marketing research, and business operations, needs a rigorous and systematic science. Current methods are ad hoc and heuristic, offer no guarantee of rigor or precision, and introduce systematic biases into downstream tasks. Large experiments on U.S. presidential election forecasts and general opinion surveys show that these biases can produce substantial deviations from real outcomes. Releases about one million generated personas for public analysis.

entries.title: Moral stereotyping in large language models
entries.tldr: Asks whether LLMs, now used to estimate public opinion and simulate moral judgments, capture the range of human moral values across cultures. Compares LLM estimates of moral values with survey data from 48 countries. Models consistently overstate moral concerns common in Western societies and understate values more prominent elsewhere, likely reflecting cultural bias in training data. Rather than offering a culturally neutral view, current models may misrepresent public sentiment and reinforce stereotypes.

entries.authors: Zeng, Yongchao, Calum Brown, and Mark Rounsevell
entries.title: Too human to model: the uncanny valley of large language models in simulating human systems
entries.tldr: Asks how the realism of LLM agents fits with the abstraction and interpretability that models of human systems need. Through a thought experiment on building a model, identifies five dilemmas: mismatched time scales, intervening in agent conversations without disrupting them, adding rules while keeping dialogue natural, balancing role consistency with role change, and understanding emergence. These dilemmas place LLM agents in an 'uncanny valley': more realistic than agents driven by rules, yet still recognizably not human.

entries.title: Evaluating the statistical realism of LLM-generated social science data
entries.tldr: Proposes judging LLM-generated social science data by whether it reproduces statistical patterns at the population level, following survey research principles. Introduces SSDataBench, which tests univariate distributions, bivariate associations, multivariate outcome prediction, life event sequences and their links to covariates on four longitudinal and three cross-sectional datasets across six domains. Under sparse conditioning, current LLMs compress the heterogeneity of real populations into simplified typological structures. Preliminary results suggest that training on domain data can improve realism at the population level.

entries.authors: Yin, Haonan, Shai Vardi, and Vidyanand Choudhary
entries.title: Fragile preferences: A deep dive into order effects in large language models
entries.tldr: Studies order effects when LLMs choose among alternatives, in resume evaluation and in a color selection task that isolates position. Models favor the first option when all options are strong and later options when quality is lower, and they show a name bias even with demographic signals controlled. An extended rational choice framework that labels preferences robust, fragile, or indifferent shows that order effects can lead to strictly inferior choices. Proposes mitigations, including using the temperature parameter to recover underlying preferences.

entries.title: Digital twins are funhouse mirrors: Five systematic distortions
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Evaluates LLM digital twins of individual people, each built from a participant's answers to more than 500 earlier questions. Across 19 preregistered studies covering 164 outcomes, such as views on hiring algorithms and willingness to spread misinformation, twin answers are compared with the real people's responses. Twins are only slightly more accurate than the base model and correlate weakly with humans, with an average correlation of 0.20. Identifies five systematic distortions: insufficient individuation, stereotyping, representation bias, ideological biases and hyper-rationality.

entries.title: How price sensitive is AI? Benchmarking LLM-generated willingness to pay in pricing analytics
entries.tldr: Benchmarks willingness to pay generated by LLMs against real values elicited with the incentive compatible Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism across four consumer product studies. Synthetic answers look economically plausible but lead to different pricing decisions: for two hedonic products they overstate willingness to pay and imply overly optimistic demand and profit, while for two utilitarian products results range from close mean agreement to large underestimation. Synthetic and real distributions differ significantly in every study, so matching means is not enough for validation.

entries.authors: Karetnikov, Nikita, Iyad Rahwan, and Davor Svetinovic
entries.title: Large language models as human proxies
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Reviews research across disciplines that uses LLMs, explicitly or implicitly, as stand-ins for humans. Notes that LLMs do not explain the mechanisms behind human behavior but may still substitute for people in applied and scientific work. Sorts existing uses into four roles: believable agents, task agents, experimental subjects and silicon samples. Comparing these roles shows that similarity to humans is not a single property, since each role supports a different scientific claim and needs its own validity criteria.

entries.title: The Challenge of Using LLMs to Simulate Human Behavior: A Causal Inference Perspective
entries.tldr: Examines a causal inference problem in using LLMs to simulate human behavior. When simulated subjects are blind to the experimental design, changing the treatment in the prompt also shifts unspecified variables and violates unconfoundedness, producing implausible results in a demand estimation benchmark against a real experiment with 40 products. Controlling for covariates hurts ecological validity, so the authors propose unblinding, which reveals the design to the LLM. Unblinding improves performance across all tested models, with and without reasoning, and complements fine-tuning.

entries.title: This human study did not involve human subjects: Validating LLM simulations as behavioral evidence
entries.tldr: Asks when LLMs used as simulated participants in social science experiments can support valid inferences about human behavior. Contrasts heuristic approaches, which use prompt engineering or fine tuning to make simulated and human responses interchangeable, with statistical calibration, which combines auxiliary human data with adjustments for gaps between simulated and observed responses. Heuristics suit exploratory work but lack the guarantees confirmatory research needs, while calibration can preserve validity and give more precise estimates at lower cost under explicit assumptions. Both depend on how well LLMs represent the relevant populations.

entries.authors: Kuric, Eduard, Peter Demcak, and Matus Krajcovic
entries.title: Synthetic Participants Generated by Large Language Models: A Systematic Literature Review
entries.tldr: Reviews 182 studies on using LLMs to simulate research participants, weighing claimed benefits such as flexibility and lower cost against mixed empirical results. Identifies four recurring problems: cognitive misalignment, distortions, misleading believability, and overfitting or contamination. Finds that fidelity gains so far are modest and that models may parrot their training data. Suggests treating synthetic participants as heuristic tools, discusses evaluation measures and roles where they may be valid, and calls for attention to professional, social and ethical concerns.

entries.title: Statistical realism is not evidence that LLMs can estimate treatment effects in social science experiments
entries.tldr: Tests whether statistical realism, meaning how closely simulated survey responses match real ones, predicts how accurately LLMs estimate treatment effects. Uses a cross-national experiment with 59,508 participants from 62 countries and three LLMs, plus two replication experiments with 20,785 participants. The link between realism and treatment effect accuracy is weak, and optimizing for realism when choosing models, prompts or populations can worsen effect estimates, especially for behavioral outcomes. Offers a diagnostic framework and argues that simulated responses and simulated treatment effects are distinct targets.

entries.authors: Kuric, Eduard, Peter Demcak, and Matus Krajcovic
entries.title: What Would GPT Click: Practical Effects of Human-AI Behavioral Misalignment and the Cost of Synthetic Participants in User Experience
entries.tldr: Tests whether GPT can stand in for human participants in UX research by asking it to predict where people click and explain why, using twelve first-click tests from real practice with 3,431 participants. Synthetic click distributions differ significantly from real data in 53% of tasks, with critical failures on visual elements and on the reasoning behind clicks. Personas, chain of thought prompting, and varied sampling settings do not meaningfully improve fidelity and mainly make outputs seem more believable.

entries.title: Synthetic Personalities: How Well Can LLMs Mimic Individual Respondents Using Socio-Economic Microdata?
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLMs can build digital twins of individual respondents from existing panel survey data. Builds twins from the German Socio-Economic Panel with three open weight models, five levels of information depth, two embedding methods and two reasoning modes, scoring over 2.1 million responses from 500 participants on 183 held out questions. Accuracy rises with information depth but levels off beyond the 75th entropy percentile, and raw dialog history beats narrative persona summaries. The best setup reaches about 78.8% accuracy and a correlation of 0.590.

entries.authors: Chen, Zihan, Di Zhu, and Lei Nico Zheng
entries.title: When Synthetic Users Fail: A Cross-Domain Benchmark of LLM-Simulated Human Survey Responses
entries.tldr: Tests when LLMs can stand in for human survey respondents, using four models from 8B parameters to frontier scale on the General Social Survey and World Values Survey. No model beats the strongest baseline without an LLM at the individual level, with the widest gap on values across cultures. Models also treat demographics as far more predictive of attitudes than they are, and larger models fix neither problem. In a segment targeting test, models exaggerate differences between segments and often point to the wrong one.

entries.title: Synthetic Data and Digital Twins: The Hype, The Facts, the Promise
entries.tldr: Reviews the empirical evidence on synthetic data and digital twins, which simulate human behavior and responses to new scenarios using structured and unstructured data. Finds that, despite some encouraging results, synthetic data currently predict human behavior poorly overall and distort it systematically. Identifies research opportunities in making synthetic data more accurate and useful and in new use cases for digital twins. Argues that researchers and practitioners should calibrate their expectations about the maximum predictivity synthetic data can reach.

entries.title: AI-Moderated Interviews for Market Research and Digital Twins Calibration
entries.tldr: Compares interviews moderated by AI, interviews moderated by humans, and static interviews for market research and for building consumer digital twins, in a preregistered study with 317 participants and three industry partners. AI moderation matches human depth, covers more themes, and recovers significantly more customer needs at equal budget, though participants sound more emotionally engaged with a human. Twins built from AI interviews predict each person's withheld responses to six marketing stimuli better than personas based only on demographics, but no better than twins built from static interviews.

entries.title: Synthetic Data in Marketing Research: How to Evaluate and When to Trust
entries.tldr: Asks when synthetic data can be trusted in marketing research. Distinguishes ungrounded LLM responses, segment personas and individual digital twins, and argues that reported twin accuracy varies mostly with the measure used. For questions missing from a fielded study, proposes a diagnostic needing no ground truth: the R² of a random forest predicting twin outputs from the twins' input data. Across 108 attitude questions (N = 3,063), screening at R² above 0.7 raises twin and human correlation by 15% and cuts poorly answered questions from 25.9% to 4.3%.

entries.title: Measuring the Digital Twin: Separating Individuation from Population Regularity in LLM Survey Twins
entries.note: no public copy yet; link goes to its citation in Netzer and Sambandam, arXiv 2609.13995

entries.title: Seeing Is Not Perceiving: When Synthetic Consumers Can and Cannot Pretest Visual Marketing
entries.tldr: Tests whether generative AI agents acting as synthetic consumers can pretest visual marketing such as logos, packaging and ads. Replicates six visual marketing experiments, varying the model (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and input format (plain text vs. JSON). Every configuration passes manipulation checks, but none reproduces more than two of the six human effects, and one reverses the human pattern. Evidence given in context moves responses toward human effects, yet even successful setups capture under half of human variation, and a "Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy" protocol guides when human panels remain necessary.

entries.title: A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Introduces Centaur, a model built by fine-tuning a language model on Psych-101, a dataset of behavior recorded trial by trial from more than 60,000 participants making over 10,000,000 choices in 160 experiments. Centaur can simulate any experiment described in natural language. It predicts the behavior of unseen participants better than existing cognitive models and generalizes to new cover stories, modified task structures, and new domains. After fine-tuning, its internal representations become aligned with human neural activity.

entries.authors: Wang, Mengxin, Dennis J. Zhang, and Heng Zhang
entries.title: Large Language Models for Market Research: A Data-Augmentation Approach
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Asks how data generated by LLMs can support conjoint analysis, given that substituting it for human responses introduces bias. Proposes a statistical data augmentation approach that combines LLM data with real data, yielding asymptotically valid estimators and a finite sample error bound. In a study of COVID-19 vaccine preferences, it reduces estimation error and saves 24.9% to 79.8% of data and costs, while naive substitution saves none. A second study on sports car choices supports the results.

entries.title: Generative Augmented Inference
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Proposes Generative Augmented Inference (GAI) for estimation that combines human labels with annotations from LLMs. Naively pooling AI and human labels introduces bias, and Prediction-Powered Inference assumes AI outputs are proxies for true labels, which generative models often violate. GAI instead treats AI outputs as informative, possibly high dimensional features for predicting human labels and models that link nonparametrically. It is asymptotically normal, beats human data alone in efficiency when AI outputs are informative, and lowers estimation error on real datasets.

entries.authors: Leng, Yan, Yunxin Sang, and Ashish Agarwal
entries.title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Addresses how to combine noisy LLM measurements of preferences and opinions that shift with the prompt, persona and model checkpoint. Proposes Human Mimicry Calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc method that learns credibility weights over elicitation variants from aggregate human benchmarks alone and does at least as well as any fixed weighting rule on the calibration data. In a market structure study with US bank card transactions and a public opinion study with Pew data, HuMCal improves alignment with human benchmarks and mostly beats heuristic baselines out of sample.

entries.title: LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings
entries.tldr: Addresses the unrealistic rating distributions LLMs produce when asked directly for numerical survey ratings. Proposes semantic similarity rating (SSR), which has the model write a free text response and maps it to a Likert distribution through embedding similarity with reference statements. On 57 personal care product surveys with 9,300 human responses, SSR reaches 90% of human test-retest reliability and keeps distributions realistic, with Kolmogorov-Smirnov similarity above 0.85. The synthetic respondents also give qualitative feedback explaining their ratings.

entries.title: LLM-SAA: LLM-persona Generated Distributions for Decision-making
entries.tldr: Proposes LLM-SAA, in which an LLM generates an estimated distribution, such as simulated consumer willingness to pay, and a decision is then optimized under that distribution. Introduces metrics that judge these generated distributions by the decisions they lead to. Tests the approach on assortment optimization, pricing and newsvendor problems. The distributions prove practically useful, especially when data is scarce, while measures that ignore the decision, such as Wasserstein distance, can be misleading.

entries.title: SYN-DIGITS: A Synthetic Control Framework for Calibrated Digital Twin Simulation
entries.tldr: Proposes SYN-DIGITS, a calibration framework inspired by synthetic control methods that corrects systematic bias in LLM digital twin simulations. It learns latent structure from twin responses and aligns them with human ground truth, running as a layer on top of any LLM simulator. A latent factor model shows when calibration succeeds. In tests of ten calibration methods across personas, LLMs and datasets, it raises correlation at the individual level by up to 50% in relative terms and cuts distributional discrepancy by 50 to 90% versus uncalibrated baselines.

entries.title: Rectification Difficulty and Optimal Sample Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys
entries.tldr: Studies how to split a fixed budget of human respondents across survey questions when an LLM can cheaply predict every answer. Building on Prediction-Powered Inference, defines a question-specific rectification difficulty and derives a closed form rule that sends more human responses where the LLM is least reliable, with meta-learning on past surveys to predict difficulty without pilot data. The framework extends to regression coefficients and conjoint partworths. On two datasets, it captures 61 to 79% of attainable efficiency gains and cuts MSE by 11.4% and 10.5%.

entries.authors: Ye, Zikun, Jiameng Lyu, and Rui Tao
entries.title: Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
entries.tldr: Studies how to split a fixed budget of noisy human labels across many tasks that use AI predictions, such as product testing or market research, when AI reliability differs by task and is unknown beforehand. Combines tuned prediction-powered inference with an upper confidence bound policy that learns task difficulty online and sends labels where AI is least reliable. On a digital twin survey with 68 tasks and over 2,000 respondents, it cuts the gap to the oracle allocation from 10 to 12% under uniform allocation to 2 to 6%.

entries.title: LLM-Powered Virtual Population for Demand Simulation and Pricing
entries.tldr: Proposes a demand simulator based on LLMs to support pricing for products described by text and images. Customers are modeled as a mixture of personas; for each persona, product and candidate price, an LLM estimates a purchase probability, and calibrated weights combine these into a distribution of aggregate demand. Prices can then be compared by expected revenue or by criteria that account for risk, such as conditional value at risk. On an online H&M fashion dataset, the calibrated simulator achieves the best overall predictive performance among the models considered.

entries.title: Distributionally Robust LLM Augmentation of Discrete Choice Models
Economic valuation of product features
entries.tldr: Proposes a market-based way to value adding or improving a product feature, defined as the difference in equilibrium profits a firm earns with and without the enhancement. Computing this requires a valid demand model plus data on competing offerings and costs. Because demand data are often unavailable or say little about a new feature, conjoint survey experiments supply the demand model. An application to digital cameras shows that these profit values differ substantially from standard welfare and willingness to pay measures.

entries.title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
entries.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1(4): 443-490
entries.tldr: Replicates 28 classic and contemporary findings with preregistered protocols, each run in about half of 125 samples totaling 15,305 participants from 36 countries and territories. Only 15 replications (54%) find a significant effect in the original direction, and the median effect size falls from d = 0.60 in the originals to 0.15. Heterogeneity across samples is modest and owes little to task order, lab versus online administration, or more versus less WEIRD cultures. Variation in effect sizes depends more on the effect studied than on the sample or setting.

entries.title: Using large-scale experiments and machine learning to discover theories of human decision-making
entries.label: natsci
entries.data_desc: Choices13k: human choice frequencies for 13,006 risky-choice problems.
entries.tldr: Asks whether large datasets and machine learning can speed the discovery of theories of human decision making. Runs the largest study of risky choice to date and analyzes it by optimizing differentiable decision theories implemented as artificial neural networks. The approach recovers historical findings, shows that existing theories can be improved, and yields a more accurate new model that retains insights from earlier research. Results also indicate that people's choices violate assumptions built into classic decision theories.

entries.title: Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.data_desc: OpinionQA: 1,498 Pew survey questions with human and model responses.
entries.tldr: Asks whose opinions language models reflect when they answer subjective questions. Uses public opinion polls to build OpinionQA, a dataset that compares LM opinions with those of 60 US demographic groups on topics from abortion to automation. Current LMs show substantial misalignment with these groups, comparable to the gap between Democrats and Republicans on climate change, and it persists even when models are steered toward a group. Models tuned with human feedback lean left, and groups such as people aged 65 and older and widowed individuals are poorly reflected.

entries.title: A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Introduces Centaur, a model built by fine-tuning a language model on Psych-101, a dataset of behavior recorded trial by trial from more than 60,000 participants making over 10,000,000 choices in 160 experiments. Centaur can simulate any experiment described in natural language. It predicts the behavior of unseen participants better than existing cognitive models and generalizes to new cover stories, modified task structures, and new domains. After fine-tuning, its internal representations become aligned with human neural activity.

entries.title: Database Report: Twin-2K-500: A Data Set for Building Digital Twins of over 2,000 People Based on Their Answers to over 500 Questions
entries.label: utd24
entries.data_desc: Four-wave surveys of 2,058 US participants, plus LLM responses.
entries.tldr: Releases a public dataset for building and testing LLM digital twins, addressing the lack of large public data on individual behavior. A representative sample of 2,058 Americans spent 2.42 hours on average answering more than 500 questions over four waves, covering demographics, psychology, economics, personality and cognition, plus replications of behavioral economics experiments and a pricing survey. The final wave repeats earlier tasks to give a retest baseline. Initial analyses suggest high data quality and support for twins that predict behavior well for individuals and groups.

entries.title: SimBench: Benchmarking the Ability of Large Language Models to Simulate Human Behaviors
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.data_desc: 20 datasets of human decisions and self-assessments.
entries.tldr: Introduces SimBench, a standardized benchmark of how faithfully LLMs simulate human behavior, unifying 20 datasets from moral decisions to economic choice drawn from a large global participant pool. The best current models score 40.80 out of 100. Performance grows log-linearly with model size but not with more inference compute, and instruction tuning helps on consensus questions while hurting on questions with diverse answers. Models struggle to simulate specific demographic groups, and simulation ability correlates most with knowledge-intensive reasoning (r = 0.939 with MMLU-Pro).

entries.title: Instructions and Guide for Diagnostic Questions: The NeurIPS 2020 Education Challenge
entries.tldr: Describes the NeurIPS 2020 Education Challenge, built on over 20 million student answers to multiple choice diagnostic math questions from the Eedi platform. Diagnostic questions are designed so that a student's chosen answer can reveal a specific misconception. The competition sets three tasks: predict which answers students give, predict which questions are high quality, and choose a personalized question sequence for each student that best predicts that student's answers.

entries.title: Scaling Synthetic Data Creation with 1,000,000,000 Personas
entries.data_desc: PersonaHub: synthetic personas and task samples.
entries.tldr: Proposes creating diverse synthetic data by prompting an LLM from the perspectives of many different personas. Introduces Persona Hub, a collection of 1 billion personas automatically curated from web data, equal to about 13% of the world's population, which act as distributed carriers of world knowledge. Demonstrates the approach by generating math and logical reasoning problems, user instructions, texts rich in knowledge, game NPCs and tools (functions). Presents the method as versatile, scalable, flexible and easy to use.

entries.title: SimGym: A Framework for A/B Test Simulation in E-Commerce with Traffic-Grounded VLM Agents
entries.tldr: Proposes SimGym, a framework that simulates A/B tests of e-commerce storefronts with vision language model agents acting in a live browser. It combines personas derived from production clickstream data, a browser agent with episodic memory and guardrails, and an evaluation that compares simulated outcome shifts with real buyer behavior. On UI theme changes from a major e-commerce platform, the agents reach 77% directional alignment with shifts in cart additions seen in real buyer traffic. This shortens experiment cycles from weeks to under an hour without exposing buyers to candidate variants.

entries.title: MatrAIx: Simulating the World with 8.3 Billion Persona Agents
entries.data_desc: 999,847 human-derived and synthetic personas with 1,290 attributes.
entries.tldr: Presents MatrAIx, infrastructure for evaluating AI systems and digital products with simulated users at population scale. It combines Persona 8B, 8.3 billion persona records over 1,290 categorical dimensions (about 1 million released), four environments (Survey, AI Chatbot, Web, App) and 1,010 tasks across more than 25 domains. In 18,189 trials on eight tasks with three LLMs, simulated feedback varies with persona, such as hesitation after a price increase, and a 400-trial check finds declared persona behavior expressed or correctly suppressed in 91.5% of trials.

entries.title: AgentPersonaBench: Benchmarking Persona-Driven User Simulation
entries.tldr: Introduces AgentPersonaBench (APB), which tests whether a persona changes what an agent actually does rather than its style or self-reported traits. Each trait is embedded, unnamed, in a full synthetic profile, and adherence is judged from actions across 2,460 tasks covering 867 traits on four surfaces: survey, chat, web, and desktop software. Among 20 frontier model configurations, the best reach 84.7% full pass adherence without persona prompting. Adherence drops across surfaces, with only 37.9% to 64.3% passing all four, and demands involving several attributes make personas harder to keep.

categories.blurb: consumer responses, behavioral fidelity, and market insights

categories.name: Content Generation and Personalization

entries.title: Frontiers: Supporting Content Marketing with Natural Language Generation
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Studies how natural language generation can draft landing page text for search engine optimization (SEO), which is usually written by hand at high cost. Proposes a semiautomated method that produces unique, humanlike text, though a human editor remains necessary. Edited machine text is nearly indistinguishable from human SEO copy on several qualities judged by people, including SEO experts. In field experiments in two industries, the machine content ranks higher in search results than content from human writers, and the approach can sharply cut production costs.

entries.title: Frontiers: Generative AI and Personalized Video Advertisements
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Tests personalized video ads made with generative AI in a mobile field experiment on WhatsApp with a large e-commerce brand selling sustainable products. Users are randomly assigned to GenAI personalized videos, personalized image ads, or generic videos, with personalization based on each person's purchase history. GenAI personalized videos raise engagement by six to nine percentage points over both baselines, and the gains hold across gender and location. Rough calculations suggest large cost savings and productivity gains, though effects may not carry over to other marketing contexts.

entries.authors: Reisenbichler, Martin, Thomas Reutterer, and David A. Schweidel
entries.title: Applying Large Language Models to Sponsored Search Advertising
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Studies how to adapt an LLM for search engine advertising. Builds an application layer on top of an open source LLM that generates ad text tailored to this setting, aiming to maximize clicks under cost per click pricing, and tests it in two empirical settings. Ads from this human-in-the-loop approach outperform both ads written by humans and ads from standard LLMs, but may raise cost per click, so advertisers must weigh better content against higher cost. Also identifies boundary conditions that limit the gains.

entries.title: Ads that Talk Back: Implications and Perceptions of Injecting Personalized Advertising into LLM Chatbots
entries.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies 9(4): Article 213
entries.tldr: Examines what happens when LLM chatbots carry personalized ads, using a chatbot that embeds personalized product ads in its responses and an experiment with 179 participants. Benchmarks show ad injection only slightly affects chatbot performance, mainly response desirability. Participants struggle to detect the ads and even prefer responses with hidden advertising, and they try to change ad settings through natural language requests rather than clicking the disclosure. Releases Phi-4-Ads, an open model fine-tuned to serve ads, with its dataset.

entries.title: Large Language Models and Creative Content Design: a case study of email marketing at Wine Access
entries.tldr: Studies whether and how a small online business, Wine Access, should use AI to create email marketing content. Runs three randomized controlled trials comparing emails written by salaried writers, by an LLM, and by a hybrid in which people edit LLM drafts, using frequentist decision theory suited to small samples. Against a control that sends no email, all three approaches roughly double gross profit from orders. Decision theory always selects an AI option over the standard human policy based on annual profit net of labor and software costs.

entries.title: The Promise of Generative AI for Personalized Persuasion
entries.tldr: Reviews how generative AI can tailor persuasive messages to individuals' preferences, needs and motivations. Explains how it helps solve the problem of identifying what to customize and surveys existing evidence on its effectiveness. Proposes a framework that classifies studies by their data sources, the complexity of their personalization methods and how they deliver personalized content. Closes with promising research directions and ethical considerations.

entries.title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
entries.tldr: Asks whether AI-generated ad images perform as well as human-made ones with real consumers, working with Taboola ahead of its GenAI Ad Maker launch. Compares 4,633 sibling ad pairs, each an AI image and a human image from the same advertiser with identical campaign settings, spanning over 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. AI images show no average disadvantage in click-through rate and outperform when they do not look AI-made. Sharper, clearer images with larger faces read as human, while aesthetics, lower warmth and intense color saturation signal AI.

entries.authors: Hu, Lin, Xueyan Yin, and Juan Feng
entries.title: Knowing Me, Telling Me: Information Design in Gen-AI Enabled Communication in Digital Marketing
Generative AI and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
entries.tldr: Measures the short term effect of generative AI on sales with large randomized field experiments on a leading cross border online retail platform. Across seven workflows added in 2023 and 2024, including customer service, product matching, advertising and seller services, GenAI raises sales by between zero and 16.3%. Gains come mainly from higher conversion rather than larger carts, return rates and ratings hold steady, and benefits are larger for less experienced consumers. The four applications with positive effects imply about $5 of annual value per consumer.

entries.title: The Impact of Visual Generative AI on Advertising Effectiveness
entries.tldr: Compares ads made by human experts, expert designs modified by visual generative AI, and ads generated entirely by AI, using latent diffusion models, a lab experiment and a field study. Ads fully generated by AI outperform both alternatives, raising clickthrough rates by up to 19% in the field, while modified ads do not beat the human benchmark. They evoke stronger emotional engagement and easier visual processing, and gains grow when AI also designs product packaging. Disclosing AI involvement cuts effectiveness by up to 31.5%.

entries.title: LLM-Generated Ads: From Personalization Parity to Persuasion Superiority
entries.tldr: Tests whether LLMs can write persuasive and personalized ads as well as human experts. In Study 1 (n=400), LLM ads tailored to openness and neuroticism perform on par with ads written by humans. In Study 2 (n=800), built on authority, consensus, cognition and scarcity appeals, participants prefer AI-generated ads 59.1% of the time, with the strongest results for authority and consensus. The AI advantage holds after a penalty for correctly detecting AI origin, and about 29% of participants choose AI content even knowing its source.

entries.title: When Machines Persuade Better Than Humans: Generative AI, Cognitive Constraints, and Promotional Effectiveness
entries.tldr: Tests whether promotional messages written by generative AI drive purchases in online food ordering, through a randomized field experiment with a chain restaurant. Compares personalized AI messages, generic AI messages, generic messages written by humans, and coupons alone. Both AI formats outperform human messages: personalized AI messages raise daily order amounts by 14.3% and generic ones by 10.4%. Generic AI messages work especially well under high cognitive load, such as at work, while personalized ones work across contexts, a pattern explained with the Elaboration Likelihood Model.

entries.authors: Fainmesser, Itay P., Dominique Olie Lauga, and Elie Ofek
entries.title: Will it Click? Advertising Strategy with Generative AI
entries.tldr: Models how generative AI changes advertising strategy when a firm can tailor a baseline ad template to each consumer, but the resulting messages may stray from the intended preference. Under monopoly, the optimal strategy gives a click probability with an inverted U shape over consumers' message preferences on a Salop circle. With two competing firms, better GenAI accuracy intensifies competition and lowers profits, while better identification of preferences does the reverse. Investments in GenAI are strategic substitutes, producing an asymmetric equilibrium.

entries.title: The Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment
entries.tldr: Measures how Google's AI Overviews affect clicks to outside websites, using a field experiment with a Chrome extension that randomly shows users regular Google Search or a version with the summaries removed. When an AI Overview appears, organic outbound clicks fall by 39.8% and searches with no click rise by 34.5%, while sponsored clicks and search frequency do not change. Users report no gain in search quality or ease of finding information. A smaller test of AI Mode suggests even larger traffic losses for publishers.

entries.title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Asks whether generative AI must homogenize content when producers compete for customers or attention. A formal game theory model shows that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, which mitigates monoculture, and that a model performing well on a benchmark in isolation may provide little value in a competitive market. Experiments with generative text and image models support the theory. The results suggest that homogenization is unlikely to persist under strong competition and that models should be evaluated across the full breadth of their output distributions.

entries.title: Long-Term Ad Memorability: Understanding & Generating Memorable Ads
entries.tldr: Studies how well people remember ads over the long term, which earlier work measured only through short recall. Releases LAMBDA, with 1,749 participants, 2,205 ads, and 276 brands, and finds that ads with fast scenes are more memorable and that ad blocker users recall fewer ads. Proposes Henry, a memorability predictor with top results on prominent datasets and strong zero shot generalization, and SEED, which trains an LLM to generate ads that score 44% higher on memorability than the originals.

entries.title: GRAVITY: A Framework for Personalized Text Generation via Profile-Grounded Synthetic Preferences
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Proposes GRAVITY, which generates synthetic preference data grounded in user profiles covering interests, values, beliefs and personality, to personalize LLM text without costly human feedback. Draws on Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Schwartz's basic values, the World Values Survey and Big Five traits to build preferred and dispreferred response pairs. On book descriptions for 400 Amazon users, it beats prompting, standard fine tuning and synthetic pairs without profile grounding, with preference gains over 4% higher than baselines. Users prefer its outputs 86% of the time.

entries.title: FSPO: Few-Shot Optimization of Synthetic Preferences Personalizes to Real Users
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Proposes FSPO, a meta-learning method that infers a user's reward function from a few labeled preferences to personalize LLM responses. It trains on over 1 million synthetic preferences generated with public LLMs, built for diversity and coherent structure so that learning transfers to real users. Across up to 1,500 synthetic users in movie reviews, education and open question answering, FSPO reaches an 87% Alpaca Eval win rate, and it wins 70% of the time with real users in a controlled human study.

entries.title: Design Your Ad: Personalized Advertising Image and Text Generation with Unified Autoregressive Models
entries.tldr: Studies joint generation of personalized ad images and ad text from users' historical clicks, instead of separate models driven by click-through rate, which reflects only average preferences. Proposes Uni-AdGen, a single autoregressive model that produces both, with a foreground perception module and instruction tuning for realism and a preference module that extracts user interests from noisy multimodal behavior, moving from coarse to fine. Also builds the PAd1M dataset and a Product Background Similarity (PBS) metric. The method outperforms baselines on general and personalized ad generation.

entries.title: Evaluating Novel Unstructured Treatments with Generative AI: A Causal Prediction Framework
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Proposes a causal prediction framework for evaluating new AI-generated marketing content before launch. Pretrained LLMs represent past content and learn how its features relate causally to outcomes, and a rejection sampling step keeps only proposed content that historical data can reliably support. In an email marketing application with 3.3 million observations across 34 campaigns, the framework improves prediction on new data and deployment performance over standard approaches. A threshold on similarity to past campaigns separates cases where prediction is reliable from cases that call for experiments.

entries.authors: Angelopoulos, Panagiotis, Kevin Lee, and Sanjog Misra
entries.title: Causal Alignment: Augmenting Language Models with A/B Tests

entries.authors: Cheng, Mengjie, Elie Ofek, and Hema Yoganarasimhan
entries.title: Balancing Engagement and Polarization: Multi-Objective Alignment of News Content Using LLMs
entries.tldr: Studies how news outlets can use LLMs to make articles more engaging while holding a chosen level of political slant. In New York Times articles, more engaging pieces tend to be more polarizing, and simple prompting or standard Direct Preference Optimization to raise engagement can also raise polarization. Proposes Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization (MODPO), which combines preference optimization with optimization over several objectives. The resulting open source model raises engagement while keeping editorial stance steady, by changing polarizing features that matter less for engagement.

entries.authors: Yin, Mingzhang, Ruijiang Gao, and Ziwei Cong
entries.title: Generative Personalization with Textual and Non-textual Data
SLM4Offer: Personalized Marketing Offer Generation Using Contrastive Learning Based Fine-Tuning
entries.tldr: Proposes SLM4Offer, which generates personalized marketing offers by fine-tuning Google's T5-Small (60M parameters) with contrastive learning. An InfoNCE loss aligns customer personas with relevant offers in a shared embedding space, reshaping the latent space during training to improve generalization. Trained and evaluated on a synthetic dataset that simulates customer behavior and offer acceptance, the model raises the offer acceptance rate by 17% over a supervised fine-tuning baseline.

entries.title: Offline-to-Online Creative Optimization with Generative Models and Adaptive Testing
entries.tldr: Addresses ad creative optimization, where evaluation rather than generation is the bottleneck. Uses a predictive model trained on historical A/B tests as a critic that ranks and refines a generative model's variants, then tests the resulting slate in an adaptive online experiment. In a 50 arm field experiment, the best generated creative beats the best human creative by 45.1% in engagement, with lifts of 46.7% and 36.2% in two further experiments. The predictor is too noisy to pick the winner offline but steers generation toward strong candidates.

entries.title: Leveraging Generative Artificial Intelligence to Create Visual Content in Digital Advertising
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Addresses two obstacles to using image generation in digital ads: finding strong visuals among countless possible creatives and keeping them aligned with the brand. Proposes a framework that pairs a generative AI model with two Bayesian neural networks and uses low cost Bayesian active learning to target performance and brand fit together. In a live campaign for an outdoor activities company, the generated visuals achieve a higher mean clickthrough rate with lower variance than a professional designer's creatives and a competing AI model optimized only for aesthetics.

entries.title: Persuasion Strategies in Advertisements
entries.venue: AAAI 2023, Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 37(1): 57-66
entries.data_desc: Ad images, persuasion labels, and segmentation masks.
entries.tldr: Studies what makes an advertisement persuasive, a question held back in computer vision by the lack of datasets labeled with persuasion strategies. Draws on social psychology and marketing to define a vocabulary of persuasion strategies and builds the first ad image corpus annotated with them, including segmentation masks for the test split. Frames strategy prediction as a multimodal learning task and proposes a multitask attention fusion model that uses other ad understanding tasks to predict strategies. Code and dataset are publicly released.

entries.authors: Ye, Zikun, Hema Yoganarasimhan, and Yufeng Zheng
entries.title: LOLA: LLM-Assisted Online Learning Algorithm for Content Experiments
entries.label: utd24
entries.data_desc: Upworthy headline A/B tests with impressions and clicks.
entries.tldr: Asks how to identify the most engaging headlines, using 17,681 headline A/B tests from Upworthy. Purely LLM approaches fall short: prompting performs poorly, and OpenAI embeddings and a fine tuned Llama-3-8B are only slightly better than random. Proposes LOLA, which pairs the best LLM approach with an Upper Confidence Bound algorithm that adjusts traffic over time to maximize clicks. LOLA beats standard A/B testing, pure bandit algorithms and LLM methods alone, especially when experimental traffic is limited.

entries.title: PVP: An Image Dataset for Personalized Visual Persuasion with Persuasion Strategies, Viewer Characteristics, and Persuasiveness Ratings
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.data_desc: Images, viewer profiles, persuasion strategies, and human persuasiveness ratings.
entries.tldr: Introduces the Personalized Visual Persuasion (PVP) dataset, built to link how persuasive an image is with information about the people who rate it. It contains 28,454 persuasive images covering 596 messages and 9 persuasion strategies, rated by 2,521 annotators whose demographics, personality traits, and values are recorded. Uses the data to build a persuasive image generator and an automatic persuasiveness evaluator, with benchmark baselines for both. Including viewers' psychological characteristics improves both generation and evaluation.

entries.title: A Large Scale Benchmark for Individual Treatment Effect Prediction and Uplift Modeling
entries.data_desc: Criteo Uplift: 14M ad-trial records with treatment, exposure, visits, and conversions.
entries.tldr: Releases a public dataset for individual treatment effect (ITE) prediction and uplift modeling, with applications such as online advertising. It holds 13.9 million samples from several randomized controlled trials, 210 times larger than earlier datasets, and sanity checks show it suits causal inference. Formalizes uplift modeling on the data with evaluation metrics and proposes synthetic response surfaces and heterogeneous treatment assignment as a general setup for ITE prediction. Benchmarks baseline uplift and ITE methods with high statistical significance.

categories.blurb: personalized content, advertising effects, and marketing outcomes

categories.name: Model and Algorithm Augmentation

entries.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
entries.label: natsci
entries.tldr: Asks what happens to generative models once text produced by LLMs makes up much of what is online. Training indiscriminately on content generated by models causes irreversible defects in which the tails of the original content distribution disappear, an effect called 'model collapse'. The effect appears in LLMs, variational autoencoders and Gaussian mixture models, and theory suggests it is common across learned generative models. Data on genuine human interactions therefore become increasingly valuable.

entries.title: How Powerful are LLMs to Support Multimodal Recommendation? A Reproducibility Study of LLMRec
entries.tldr: Reproduces LLMRec, which prompts an LLM with user-item interactions, item metadata and candidates from multimodal recommenders to build an augmented dataset for training a final recommender. Replication with the original and reconstructed data reveals serious problems in the reported recommendation performance. Benchmarks suggest multimodal LLMs may help more than unimodal ones, while comparisons with other multimodal recommenders, LLM-based methods and an extra dataset give results inconsistent with the original paper. Also analyzes how the augmentation changes the topology of the user-item graph.

entries.title: Regurgitative Training: The Value of Real Data in Training Large Language Models
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Studies regurgitative training, in which a new LLM is trained on data generated by itself or by other LLMs. In machine translation, fine-tuning on generated data clearly hurts performance, which links to higher error rates and lower lexical diversity than real data. Three mitigations, favoring better generated data, mixing data from several LLMs, and favoring generated data closest to real data, help but do not close the gap with real data. In creative ideation, preference fine-tuning with human feedback on generated ideas improves quality.

entries.title: Jump Start or False Start? A Theoretical and Empirical Evaluation of LLM-initialized Bandits
entries.tldr: Tests when synthetic preference data from LLMs helps warm start contextual bandits, by adding random and label flipping noise to the training data. In aligned domains, warm starts stay effective up to 30% corruption, lose their edge near 40% and hurt above 50%; under systematic misalignment, LLM priors can give higher regret than a cold start even without noise. Theory separates the two error sources and gives a sufficient condition for warm starts to win. Across conjoint datasets and LLMs, estimated alignment predicts whether warm starting helps.

entries.title: Automating the B2B Salesperson Pricing Decisions: A Human-Machine Hybrid Approach
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Builds a model of each salesperson at a B2B aluminum retailer that learns and automatically applies that person's pricing policy. In a field experiment, showing salespeople their own model's price in real time raises profits on treated quotes by 11% versus control, despite the model lacking the salesperson's private information. The model usually earns more, but salespeople do better on unusual or complex quotes. A hybrid in which a random forest routes each quote to the model or the salesperson yields higher profits than either alone.

entries.authors: Mysore, Sheshera, Andrew McCallum, and Hamed Zamani
entries.title: Large Language Model Augmented Narrative Driven Recommendations
entries.tldr: Addresses narrative driven recommendation, where users describe their preferences and context in long, detailed requests, a task with little training data. Uses few-shot prompting of LLMs to write synthetic narrative queries from user-item interactions, whose reviews often describe preferences and context. Retrieval models are then trained on these synthetic queries together with the interaction data. Small retrieval models trained this way outperform other retrieval and LLM baselines on narrative driven recommendation.

entries.authors: Alamdari, Parand A., Yanshuai Cao, and Kevin H. Wilson
entries.title: Jump Starting Bandits with LLM-Generated Prior Knowledge
entries.label: mlnlp
entries.tldr: Proposes using an LLM to jump start contextual bandits for recommendation by prompting it to generate a pretraining dataset of approximate human preferences. Because LLMs absorb human knowledge and preferences from text, this initialization reduces online learning regret and the cost of collecting training data. Validates the approach in two bandit setups: one where an LLM acts as the oracle and one using real data from a conjoint survey.

entries.authors: Ye, Zikun, Hema Yoganarasimhan, and Yufeng Zheng
entries.title: LOLA: LLM-Assisted Online Learning Algorithm for Content Experiments
entries.label: utd24
entries.tldr: Asks how to identify the most engaging headlines, using 17,681 headline A/B tests from Upworthy. Purely LLM approaches fall short: prompting performs poorly, and OpenAI embeddings and a fine tuned Llama-3-8B are only slightly better than random. Proposes LOLA, which pairs the best LLM approach with an Upper Confidence Bound algorithm that adjusts traffic over time to maximize clicks. LOLA beats standard A/B testing, pure bandit algorithms and LLM methods alone, especially when experimental traffic is limited.

entries.title: Integrating Large Language Models Into Recommendation via Mutual Augmentation and Adaptive Aggregation
entries.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing 20(1): 77–89
entries.tldr: Proposes Llama4Rec, a framework that combines an LLM with a conventional recommendation model. Conventional models mine collaborative and sequential signals but struggle with sparse data and long tail items, while LLMs use rich text but miss those signals. Llama4Rec applies data augmentation to the conventional model and prompt augmentation to the LLM, then an adaptive aggregation module merges their predictions. Experiments on three datasets show significant gains in recommendation performance.

entries.authors: Huang, Shaoqin, Hu Qin, and Yue Wang
entries.title: Mining novel customer needs for product design from user-generated content through large language model-enabled data augmentation and ensemble learning
entries.tldr: Addresses detecting novel customer needs in user-generated content such as online product reviews, where such needs are rare and mixed with noisy or irrelevant text. Uses the open source LLaMA model to generate diverse positive samples that ease class imbalance, then trains several BERT classifiers on different subsets of the augmented data and combines their predictions by hard voting. On Amazon laptop reviews, the framework beats standard baselines in recall and F1 score, which helps ensure valuable insights for product design are not missed.

entries.authors: Ludwig, Jens, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Ashesh Rambachan
entries.title: Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework
entries.tldr: Offers an econometric framework for using LLMs in empirical economics in two settings.
